$comment: The claims ladder of proofs/README.md, declared as DATA so a registry can read it
rather than parse prose. Hand-authored and never generated: the point of the manifest is
that a human decided which rung each claim sits on, and a generator would only be able to
restate what the code already says.
`level` is a CLOSED set — proved | tested | assumed | policy — and the four map onto the
README's four rungs: proved, differentially tested, assumed-and-stated, and not-claimed.
A `policy` entry is an exclusion carrying its reason, because an unstated exclusion reads,
to whoever finds it later, as a claim that failed.
A `proved` entry names its lemma and the prover pin so an evidence check can resolve the
lemma in the named module and the pin in the named file. Nothing here is checkable by
reading this file alone, and that is the intended shape: the manifest says where to look,
the proof leg (proofs/check.ps1) is what looks.
Every later proof phase in this repository appends its claims here rather than starting a
second manifest.
Phase 790 appended the disclosure-fold claims (ids prefixed `disclosure-`); the five headline
lemmas are one `proved` entry each, so an evidence check resolves them by name.
Phase 793 appended the tool-gate claims (ids prefixed `toolgate-`): the four lemmas, the
differential host, the two opaque authority predicates, and the policy entries that say what the
envelope does not bind and where the approval-by-class keying is decided.
Phase 792 appended the model-input claims (ids prefixed `model-input-`): three `proved` entries,
one per headline lemma. Note what is deliberately NOT among them - there is no claim, at any
level, about what a language model does with the rendering, and none about the transport beyond
the `policy` entries that say so. Those two are recorded as exclusions rather than omitted
outright because this file's own rule is that an unstated exclusion reads, to whoever finds it
later, as a claim that failed.
Phase 795 appended the taint-flow claims (ids prefixed `taint-`), on the same rule: the seven
headline lemmas are one `proved` entry each. The `subject` field below enumerates the 787 and
790 models only and was left as it stood; the claims are what a registry reads, and each names
its own module.
Note what `taint-inferred-lineage-fallback` and `taint-hostile-operator` are doing on the
`policy` rung. Both are things Phase 795 deliberately does NOT claim, and the temptation was to
omit them entirely. That would be the exact mistake the third paragraph above names: an
unstated exclusion reads, to whoever finds it later, as a claim that failed. They are absent
from every rung that asserts coverage, which is what matters, and present on the rung whose
whole job is to say so.
Phase 788 appended the Elmish runtime claims (ids prefixed `elmish-ring-` and `elmish-sub-`): the
ring's headline theorem and its named corollaries, the diff's seven lemmas, one `tested` entry per
differential host (BOTH runtimes, because the runtime ships to both), the capacity floor as a
`proved` entry rather than an `assumed` one - 788.D reconciled the floor to the proof's precondition
in the same phase, so nothing is left assumed - and the policy entries that say what the two models
do not reach (the dispatch loop around the ring; the effects `change` runs).
subject: the proved models under proofs/: ToolUp.Remoting.Decode - the combinator algebra over the closed MessagePack value model (Phase 787); the disclosure algebra - DisclosureEgress.evaluate plus the population fold PopulationDisclosure.fold / valuesWithheld / disclosedStats (Phase 790); and the AI tool gate - ToolGate.decideDeclared, AIToolRegistry.ListAccessible and the dispatch-site re-check over the declared ToolEffect class (Phase 793); and the model-input value - the closed value every provider call is given, its smart constructor, the assembly a caller folds over it and the pure render (Phase 792); and the taint flow - the TaintLabel lattice, the labelled transform algebra fold and DisclosureTaint.analyze's conjunction (Phase 795); and the Elmish runtime's ring buffer and subscription diff - RingBuffer<'item> proved a FIFO queue through every grow, and Sub.Internal.diff / NewSubs.calculate / Fx.change proved to start, stop and keep exactly what their comment says, on the shortcut path too (Phase 788)

fstar-pinned.reproducibility: proof hints no longer exist in this prover, so the pin, a margin on --z3rlimit, and --quake 3 over three cold runs are what stand in for them

claims.statement: Given a parsed value, no combinator and no decoder built from them can diverge, throw, or reach a state that is neither an accept nor a named refusal. Quantified over ALL decoders, not one lemma per combinator, so it covers anything a consumer or a generator composes out of the algebra.
Which outcome, for which input, with the exact refusal - expected text, found text and path. The failure classification is exhaustive rather than merely non-empty.

The element accessor that both the positional-field and the index combinator are built from returns a value strictly smaller than its input, by the value model's own size measure. A decoder descending through it cannot recur forever, and not because of a depth counter.

evidence.note: carried in element_at's REFINED RETURN TYPE, so every descent consumes it at the call site

claims.statement: The integer width rule is about INFORMATION, not signed range: a negative value never decodes into an unsigned target and fits a signed target exactly when it clears its minimum; a source no wider than its target always survives, sign reinterpretation included; a source wider than its target must fit its range; and the rule decides for every width class.

On a reader-producible value, an Int32 accept implies the payload carries no more than thirty-two bits of information - the union of the signed and unsigned 32-bit ranges. It deliberately does NOT imply the payload sits in Int32's signed range, because a negative decimal word arrives unsigned and the host's cast reinterprets it. That union is exactly the set on which the cast is a bijection.

evidence.premise: value_wf - the payload is within the width class its format byte declared. The one-pass reader produces only such values by construction; see the assumption `well-formedness-not-enforced-by-type`.

claims.statement: Over a reference API-record vocabulary - a nested record with a string, a bounded integer and a flag - the encoding of any value decodes, and decodes back to the value it started from. Not merely 'decodes to something': the decoder can never refuse traffic its own encoder produced.

The extracted model and the shipped algebra decode every covered wire-corpus case and every refuse-path mutation to the same outcome class, the same value, the same runtime type and the same refusal message. This is the only thing that says the proved model is about the code that runs.

the extracted model agrees with production over every refuse-path mutation

claims.statement: The committed oracle is byte-identical to a fresh extraction from the checked module. Without this the committed file would be a claim; with it, a checked one.

A committed go-red case hands the model a bridge that has forgotten the source width class, and asserts the comparison catches it. It catches four cases and every one is the width rule losing. A differential never shown to fail agrees with whatever it is shown.

cases: the differential CATCHES a bridge that forgets the source width - the go-red case
and the width rule is what it catches

claims.statement: The extractor and the F# compiler are trusted. The theorem is about the model; the code that runs is the extraction, and nothing verifies that the extraction preserves semantics.
claims.mitigation: the differential host runs the EXTRACTION, not the model, so an extraction defect that changes behaviour on any corpus payload is caught there

claims.statement: The value-to-model bridge in the differential host is hand-written. A defect in it would make the comparison compare the wrong thing.
claims.mitigation: short and case-for-case on purpose, and the committed go-red bridge beside it exercises the one field most likely to be got wrong

claims.statement: The extractor's F# backend ships no runtime, so the nine names it references are supplied by a hand-written shim.
claims.mitigation: small enough to read in a minute; the byte-diff means a model change reaching for a tenth name fails the leg rather than compiling against a widened shim

claims.statement: Three payload facts come from the host rather than the model: a string's length, a binary payload's length, and a float's rendered text. Recomputing any of them would introduce a second implementation free to disagree with the host's - and for string length it demonstrably would, the two runtimes counting different units.
claims.mitigation: carried as data on the value model, so the model's refusals quote the host's own numbers

claims.statement: The value model admits an integer whose payload exceeds its declared width class. The one-pass reader cannot produce one, but nothing here enforces it.
claims.mitigation: the lemmas that need it carry it as an explicit premise rather than assuming it away

claims.statement: Proof hints were removed from this prover, so the usual way to pin an SMT search is unavailable. The pinned release and its bundled solver, a margin on the resource limit, and three cold runs under --quake 3 are evidence of stability, not a guarantee of it.
The bytes-to-value pass is OUT of the theorem.
claims.reason: it is bounded - length against remaining on every length-prefixed read, and a depth ceiling - but bounded is not proved. This is the one place a binary-format proof framework would apply if it is ever wanted. A payload the reader itself refuses never reaches either decoder, and the differential skips it rather than pretending otherwise.

claims.statement: The System.Text.Json decode path is OUT.
claims.reason: its value carrier is undecided - the current JSON value model's numeric case cannot carry a 64-bit integer past 2^53, an exact decimal, or the source width

claims.statement: The reflection decode path is OUT, by construction rather than by omission.
claims.reason: it is an interpreter over an open, possibly recursive type graph walked with a mutable cursor, so 'total on every input' is not a well-formed statement about it - the input includes the type graph. That asymmetry is the whole argument for the closed value model.

claims.statement: One narrowing is unrefusable at the decoder.
claims.reason: the writer compacts a 64-bit value into bytes that ARE a well-formed 32-bit one - the shape a decimal's sign word travels in. The value model faithfully carries a 32-bit source and the information rule admits it, correctly, since refusing it would refuse every negative decimal the corpus pins. Closing it needs a writer that never compacts across a sign boundary, which is a wire break.

claims.statement: A trailing element past a record's declared fields is accepted, not refused.
claims.reason: a record decoder reads the positions it declares and ignores what follows, in agreement with the reflection reader. That is what keeps an additive wire change non-breaking, and it is the one evolution property this wire has.

claims.statement: A decoded value is well-typed. It is not authorised, not tenant-scoped and not semantically valid.
claims.reason: those are other boundaries' obligations; a decode theorem that implied them would be claiming something it cannot see

claims.statement: The date-only and time-only primitives have no combinator, so no model.
claims.reason: one of the two hosts' readers refuses both types outright, so a primitive for them would decode on one host and not the other. This ships a cross-host algebra or it ships nothing.

claims.statement: A record still decoding through the reflection path is outside every claim above.
claims.reason: the algebra is an opt-in replacement for a decoder that already works; the shipped default is unchanged

claims.statement: For any ranking, any total verdict function and any policy assignment, no fact whose verdict is not-disclosable appears in the disclosed list.

The withheld count and the withheld projection are functions of the verdict list alone - the count is the number of not-disclosable verdicts and the projection is countBy-then-sortBy over their policy refs. The relational corollary states it over two rankings whose facts may differ in every field and even in TYPE: pointwise-equal verdicts give an identical projection, so no withheld fact's identity, rank or value was consulted.
Every disclosed (rank, fact) has fact at one-based position rank of the input ranking. A withheld member leaves a gap; a contiguous renumbering cannot satisfy this.

When anything was withheld, the gated summary's minimum, maximum and mean are absent; when nothing was, the summary is returned untouched; the existence-level fields ride through in both cases; and the gate fires exactly when some verdict denied. The biconditional is over the gate's ACTION - it does not say an absent magnitude implies a withheld member, since a summary over nothing comparable carries none to begin with.

Two rankings that agree on every disclosable fact and on every verdict yield IDENTICAL PopulationDisclosure records - the same disclosed list, the same withheld count, the same withheld projection - whatever the withheld facts' identities or values. No observation of the fold's output distinguishes one withheld population from another.

Which verdict, for which classification: Surfaceable is always disclosable, Internal never (naming the classification as its policy ref), and Restricted exactly when the resolver answers Some true - Some false and None both deny, so an unknown policy ref can never fail open. The conservative default denies every Restricted fact at every surface.

evidence.note: supporting, not one of the five: it is what ties the verdicts the fold consumes to the predicate that produces them

claims.statement: The extracted model and the shipped fold agree, on every ranking the three door packs pin (reproduced as data) and on 400 generated rankings with generated verdicts, on the disclosed list, the withheld projection and the gated summary AT ONCE; and the extracted predicate agrees with the shipped one over every classification, resolver and surface. This is the only thing that says the proved model is about the code that runs.

A committed go-red oracle renumbers the disclosed ranks contiguously - the tidy-looking mistake that reports the third-best as the second-best - and the comparison is asserted to catch it, with the mechanism pinned on a three-member ranking (true ranks 1 and 3 against the oracle's 1 and 2). A differential never shown to fail agrees with whatever it is shown.

cases: the differential CATCHES an oracle that renumbers ranks contiguously - the go-red case
and the true-rank gap is what it catches

claims.statement: The theorem is about the FOLD, and the fold gates a summary the store computed over the WHOLE matched population. A restricted member ranked below the ceiling still contributed to that summary's Mean, and under a highest-first ranking can BE its Minimum. What is proved is that the gate acts on the summary exactly when it acts on the members; what is NOT proved, or claimed, is that a magnitude the gate lets through carries no information about a member the caller was never returned. The shipped code calls this a floor, not a proof, and so does this entry.
claims.mitigation: when ANY member of the ranking is withheld the whole magnitude block goes, so the residual is confined to members outside the ranking the caller asked for; a whole-population disclosure probe is a different capability

claims.statement: The ordering List.sortBy fst sorts the withheld projection by is host-supplied to the model as a before: string -> string -> bool, because F* has no string comparison that extracts to Prims alone. Every lemma holds for ANY ordering; what the model does not verify is that the host's ordinal comparison is the one the shipped code uses.
claims.mitigation: the differential compares the projection's ORDER as part of the withheld projection, so a host ordering that disagreed with List.sortBy would fail the leg on any ranking withheld under two policies

claims.statement: The Fact-to-model and PopulationStats-to-model bridges in the differential host are hand-written. A defect in either would make the comparison compare the wrong thing.
claims.mitigation: short and case-for-case on purpose: a fact is its id plus itself as the opaque payload, a summary is its three magnitudes plus itself as the opaque existence-level rest, so the read-back is a structural comparison of production's own records

claims.statement: That every door CALLS disclosedStats before reporting a summary is OUT of the theorem.
claims.reason: the theorem is about what the fold computes, not about who calls it; a summary type does not force the call, and the obligation is stated on the not-claimed rung of proofs/README.md, where the door packs are named as the evidence that the two shipped doors do

claims.statement: Statistical disclosure control is OUT. The theorem says nothing about what a determined reader could infer from a count, a period range or a freshness histogram, nor from the magnitudes of a ranking with nothing withheld.
claims.reason: the disclosure vocabulary is a declared classification enforced at egress, not an inference-control regime, and the shipped code's honesty boundary says so in the same words

claims.statement: For any RBAC predicate, any grant-liveness predicate, any ToolPolicy and any registry, no tool whose declared effects exceed the policy's ceiling is listed: under a bounded ceiling every listed tool's every declared effect has a class the ceiling names, and an undeclared tool is listed only when the policy admits undeclared tools. The supporting equality says an admitting verdict is EXACTLY the two authority predicates answering yes and the declaration sitting within the ceiling.

A tool is in the list exactly when it is in the registry and the decision admits it. Nothing the decision refused reaches the list, and nothing it admits is dropped - the list filter and the decision are one function, not two that happen to agree.

If the dispatch-site re-check admits the name the model produced - looked up by authored name or provider alias, then decided - the list the model was offered carries a tool of that name. A forged, hallucinated or replayed name the list would have refused is refused at dispatch too. This is the 'two gates that must agree share their whole decision' comment on ListAccessible, as a lemma.

A tool declaring Egress to any destination is refused under every bounded ceiling that does not name the egress class, whatever else it declares and whatever the two authority predicates answer. This is the go-red property in proof form: a gate that dropped Egress before deciding would violate it.

The extracted model and the shipped gate agree on the VERDICT for every in-tree tool the host can reach (the narrative and cross-module built-ins, the three fact tools, the sample client tool) and for 60 generated tools, under 28 generated policies including the external-principal view of each, 11 generated callers and their grant predicates; on the LISTED SET, in order, under every policy and caller; and on the DISPATCH answer by authored name, by provider alias and for an unknown name. This is the only thing that says the proved model is about the code that runs.

A committed go-red gate drops Egress from a declaration before deciding - measuring a tool by what it reads rather than where it reaches - and the comparison is asserted to catch it, with the mechanism pinned on one tool declaring only Egress under the read-only policy: production and the honest oracle refuse naming the egress, the blind gate admits. A differential never shown to fail agrees with whatever it is shown.

cases: the differential CATCHES a gate that ignores Egress - the go-red case
and egress under a read-only ceiling is what it catches

claims.statement: RBAC (isToolSourcePermittedFor over the caller's permission map, its Read/Write/Admin hierarchy and the SDK-reserved-namespace exemption) and grant liveness (moduleGrantGate over the request's consent stamps) are host-supplied predicates the model takes as total arrows. Every lemma holds for any pair; what the model does not verify is what either answers. They are earlier phases' decisions, and modelling them would introduce a second implementation free to disagree with the host's.
claims.mitigation: the differential host passes production's own isToolSourcePermittedFor and generated grant predicates to BOTH sides, so the verdicts compared include the two refusals those predicates produce

claims.statement: The bridge from the shipped types to the model's is hand-written: an effect case for case, a declared set as its sorted list, a policy's ceiling and undeclared flag, a registered tool's name, alias, source and folded declaration. A defect in it would make the comparison compare the wrong thing.
claims.mitigation: short and case-for-case on purpose; the go-red gate beside it is built from production's OWN decision over a perturbed declaration, so the comparison is known to see a declaration defect

claims.statement: The effect envelope refuses what a DECLARED tool body reaches for through the SDK's seams - a host capability through ToolEffectEnvelope.guardInvoke, an outbound request through guardEgress, a scoped write through guardWrite. An executor that constructs its own HttpClient, opens a socket or writes a file directly is outside every check, exactly as it is outside the composition capability gate. Nothing short of process-level isolation closes that, and nothing here claims to.
claims.mitigation: the verified composition profile makes the declaration mandatory, so under it every in-tree tool is bound at the seams; a tool's own outbound call is the one place an author must route through guardEgress, and the envelope test pack pins that a ReadFacts tool cannot send through it

claims.statement: The policy ceiling is expressed over effect CLASSES, with payloads erased; a ceiling cannot say 'egress to api.example.com but nowhere else'.
claims.reason: a ceiling that could only name exact destinations or scopes could never say 'no egress at all', which is the sentence a policy most needs to say; the exact payload is checked at the moment of use by the envelope, which refuses Egress 'b' under a declaration of Egress 'a'

claims.statement: The human-in-the-loop approval hold is keyed on effect class through ToolPolicy.RequireApproval and ToolApprovalDispatch.requirementByClass, in FRONT of the deployment's own IToolApprovalPolicy: a tool declaring a held class is held whatever that policy says about it by name, and a tool declaring none falls through to it unchanged.
claims.reason: a per-tool name list widens silently the moment a module registers a new tool; a class-keyed hold binds the new tool by what it declares. The composition and its rationale are in docs/migrations/793-tool-effect-class.md and docs/ai/extending.md; the external-principal ceiling (ToolPolicy.ExternalPrincipalCeiling) is the same keying applied to an agent's grants, default-deny by class

claims.statement: A client-resident tool's body runs in the browser and is OUT of the envelope.
claims.reason: the envelope is an ambient server-side value around Execute, and a client-resident dispatch never calls Execute; the browser-side body is bound by the client-tool allowlist seam instead, and the gate's list and dispatch decisions apply to both locations alike

claims.statement: For ANY candidate store - whatever verdicts it carries, whatever scopes those verdicts were resolved for, in any mixture - the assembled model input holds only facts whose disclosure verdict is affirmative AND whose scope is the caller's resolved one. An affirmative verdict for another scope is not permission and is refused by the same invariant. Nothing about the store has to be checked in advance: the arm that would break the invariant is the arm that refuses.

Rendering introduces nothing the value does not carry. The turns pass through untouched; the system prompt is exactly the blocks' text joined on the composer's separator, and absent when there are no blocks, so a call that sent no system prompt is byte-for-byte unchanged; every id the leak differential reports is genuinely present in the rendering and genuinely undeclared in the value; and every candidate id that is present and undeclared IS reported, so an empty report means what a reader takes it to mean. The relational companion is the stronger half: two values agreeing on their blocks and turns render identically whatever their facts, passages and tool results are, so the renderer cannot read the fact list at all.

evidence.note: substring containment is host-supplied; every clause holds for ANY containment test - see the assumption `model-input-containment-host-supplied`

claims.statement: Two fact stores that agree on every fact disclosable for the resolved scope assemble to the SAME value, and therefore to the same rendering and the same bytes. The withheld facts are quantified away entirely - the stores may differ in count, identity, content and policy, and no observation of what the provider is shown distinguishes one from the other. The renderer that turns admitted facts into the block a reader sees is universally quantified, so this holds for every renderer a caller might write, including one that prints each admitted fact's content verbatim.

evidence.premise: the assembly hands the block renderer WHAT WAS ADMITTED, not the store. A renderer handed the store could not satisfy this, which is why the theorem is stated over the assembly rather than over render alone.

claims.statement: The retrieved-passage half of admissibility is CHECKED, not enforced. The shipped constructor accepts a passage whatever its content-gate result, so that clause is proved as a premise on the add and as a total decision procedure a caller may run - never as the unconditional invariant the fact clause is. A caller that never asks can hold a value carrying a failed passage, and nothing in the type stops it. `NotGated` is recorded honestly: it says the gate did not run, never that it passed.
claims.mitigation: the decision procedure is proved total and is compared against the shipped predicate on every differential case, so a caller that DOES ask gets an answer the theorem covers

claims.statement: Scope resolution is assumed correct. The scope is a caller-supplied string; the model compares it and never derives it, so every claim above is conditional on that string being the scope the caller is entitled to, and on the verdict having been resolved against the same one. This is the load-bearing assumption of the whole input-side claim.
claims.retired_by: the phase that makes scope resolution a single choke point
claims.mitigation: the scope is compared rather than ignored, so an affirmative verdict resolved for a DIFFERENT scope is refused by `admissible_by_construction` - the assumption is about which string is right, not about whether the string is consulted

claims.statement: The tool-effect side is assumed, not checked here. This theorem is about what goes in. The plain-English sentence a reader wants additionally needs that the tools a model may call cannot fetch what the input side refused, and nothing in this module can see that. It is recorded as an assumption rather than an exclusion because it is load-bearing for the claim rather than merely outside it: a tool that read freely would defeat everything proved above without contradicting any lemma in it.

The shipped module ships the constructors; the fold over a candidate set is what each caller writes around them. The model states the theorem over that fold, because a statement about one constructor call says nothing about a store - but a caller free to write a different fold is free to write one these lemmas do not describe.
claims.mitigation: the differential host runs PRODUCTION's constructors in the same sequence the model folds, so a divergence between the modelled assembly and the shipped constructors is caught; what it cannot catch is a caller elsewhere folding differently

claims.statement: The substring containment the leak differential asks for is host-supplied, because F* has no substring test that extracts to Prims alone. Every clause holds for ANY containment test; what the model does not verify is that the host's test is the one the shipped code uses.
claims.mitigation: the differential compares the leak list itself on every case, so a host test that disagreed with the shipped `Contains` would fail the leg on any case whose rendering names an undeclared candidate

claims.statement: The value-to-model bridge in the differential host is hand-written. A defect in it would make the comparison compare the wrong thing. The turn type is additionally NARROWED - the model carries the three fields rendering reads, and the bridge passes the production record through unchanged.
claims.mitigation: case-for-case on purpose, and the block renderer is SHARED between the two sides: the model's facts are mapped back to production records and handed to production's own renderer, so no second implementation can quietly disagree

claims.statement: The extracted value, constructor, assembly and renderer agree with the shipped ones over a pinned corpus and 150 generated cases, on the assembled value, the constructor's refusal wording, the mirrored tool-result record, the rendering, every byte of the rendered text and the leak differential over it AT ONCE. The migration seam every provider entry lifts through is compared on its own first. A 250-subject population is offered as a store with three facts admissible and 247 denied three different ways, and exactly three enter the value, exactly three reach the rendering, and none of the other 247 appears in the bytes a provider would be handed. Noninterference is run as well as proved: every case with something withheld is replayed against a store that replaces the withheld facts wholesale, and nothing a provider boundary observes may move.

A committed go-red oracle renders one fact the constructor refused - the mistake a plausible reimplementation reaches by rendering from the store rather than from what was admitted - and the comparison is asserted to catch it on EVERY case that has a withheld fact to leak, not merely on one. claims.statement: The transport is OUT. That the rendered bytes reach a provider unaltered, and that the provider sends what it was given, are not claimed at any level.
claims.reason: `render` is where this theorem stops - it produces the two arguments the provider interface takes, and everything past that boundary is another component's obligation

claims.statement: The language model is OUT, entirely. Nothing here says what it does with the bytes, what it answers, or what it may have learned elsewhere.
claims.reason: keeping the model outside the trusted set is the whole point of stating the input side this precisely; a theorem that implied anything about its behaviour would be claiming something it cannot see

claims.statement: How a builder obtained a block's text is OUT. By the time the value holds it, it is data.
claims.reason: the split is deliberate - assembly keeps its IO, rendering is total and effect-free, and it is the second half a theorem can be stated about. Which store a builder read and whether it was entitled to is that builder's own obligation.

claims.statement: What a reader could deduce from the facts that WERE admitted, from their count, or from their absence is OUT.
claims.reason: the disclosure vocabulary is a declared classification enforced at the boundary, not an inference-control regime - the same honesty boundary the disclosure fold's ladder states in the same words

claims.statement: The taint-label join is associative and has bottom as a two-sided identity ON THE NOSE; it is commutative, idempotent and an upper bound of both its parts up to label equality, which is set equality and is what the shipped label's own equality computes. join_is_least adds the other half, so the join is the LEAST upper bound and the order is a lattice order rather than merely some order; below_is_sub proves the shipped definition of that order is the same relation the model reasons with.

Raise any source's declared label - one of them, all of them - and the label the pipeline's output carries can only rise. label_never_falls is the per-node companion: along the pipeline the label is non-decreasing at every node, because the fold only ever joins, so nothing in the transform algebra can lower a label.

For any pipeline in the transform algebra, any two input assignments differing ONLY in one contributor's data, and any output whose computed label does not carry that contributor - the outputs are IDENTICAL. Quantified over every semantics of the transform cases, so it is not a claim about what the transforms happen to compute but about what they are able to READ, which is the thing the label tracks.

evidence.note: the semantics is a parameter rather than a definition, which is why the model needs nothing from the production executor

claims.statement: The exception stated as the exception. If a label carried a contributor and the narrowed label does not, the routine's entitlement predicate cleared it - and where that contributor's policy declares a contributor scope, the routine's accepting scopes name that scope. So one contributor's consent can never lower another's label, and nothing else lowers a label at all (label_never_falls, above, is that second half over the algebra).

An empty inherited-policy set means every taint-propagating source that reached the target was DROPPED somewhere on its derivation, and every drop anywhere in that derivation was made by a routine entitled to make it. So the gate's single condition - this list is empty - is exactly 'a path satisfies every contributing scope's policy'.

evidence.note: every_drop_is_entitled is UNCONDITIONAL - it holds at every node of every derivation, with no premise, because the only way a ref leaves a node is the narrowing

claims.statement: The flow half over a SEQUENCE. A room emits an ordered trace of releases and slice_tr q is one contributor's view of it, with scoped segments that contributor is outside dropping out. Two runs whose assignments differ only in another contributor's data give the same slice - the same values, in the same order, and the same number of them. Ordering and count are covered because the conclusion is list equality, not equality of one output.

The obligation is on whoever supplies the rebuild function; the lemma is that supplying it SUFFICES, which is the whole content of the refinement pattern - the work is exhibiting the function, and this is what the work buys.

claims.statement: The attacker is honest-but-curious. The theorem is about what a composed computation can carry to whom: it assumes the parties run the computation as composed and observe what they are given. It says nothing about an adversary who deviates from the protocol, and nothing about one who can read memory, modify a binary, or reach the data outside the computation at all.
claims.mitigation: it is the same attacker model the borrowed trace form was proved under, and it is named on the ladder's assumed rung rather than left to be inferred, because containment read as operator-proof is the one overclaim this ladder exists to prevent

claims.statement: The declassification routines' own correctness is assumed, not proved. Whether an aggregation-over-k or a noise addition actually loses attribution is the routine's business. This is a proof about WALLS, not about routines: declassify_only_lowers says a label was lowered only by a routine the contributor accepted; it does not say the routine deserved to be accepted.
claims.mitigation: the entitlement is per-contributor and fail-closed, so a routine nobody accepted clears nothing at all - which bounds the damage a bad routine can do to the contributors who accepted it

claims.statement: Inference across declassified outputs is out of the theorem. A release whose computed label carries a contributor is outside the trace lemma by construction: that release is a declassification, the contributor's data did influence it, and that is what a declassification means. What a determined reader could reconstruct across a SEQUENCE of such releases is a budget question, and a budget is a metered allowance, never a proof.
claims.mitigation: the boundary is explicit rather than implicit - q_free_of is taken before each release's own declassification, so the lemma's premise names exactly the releases it does not cover

claims.statement: The storage scope is assumed resolved. The theorem is about the computation's information flow; where the inputs and outputs are held, and under whose control, is a separate obligation it takes as discharged.

The derivation is modelled as a TREE. Production walks a graph with a memo table and a cycle guard. A memo cannot change a value; the content-addressed store is acyclic, and a tree is the acyclic case unfolded - where a graph shares an upstream the unfolding visits it twice and joins the same refs into the same label, which is immaterial under set equality.
claims.mitigation: the differential checks the unfolding against the real walk on every fixture rather than leaving it asserted, and the host mirrors the cycle guard so a malformed graph cannot diverge there either

claims.statement: The theorem is about the LABEL, not the ordered ref list. Production keeps the inherited refs in nearest-declared-first order so the single deny ref it reports is unchanged from Phase 562. Order is a presentation fact about a refusal message; the label is the set, and the set is what is reasoned about.
claims.mitigation: the differential compares against production's own InheritedLabel, which is the set, so the comparison and the theorem are about the same value

claims.statement: The bridges in the differential host are hand-written. A label crosses as its own contents and returns through the shipped constructor; a transform crosses as its case; a fact's derivation is unfolded from the graph, mirroring production's private source-policy test rather than reaching for it. A defect in any of them would make the comparison compare the wrong thing.
claims.mitigation: short and case-for-case on purpose, and the committed go-red oracle beside them exercises the one field most likely to be got wrong; a bridge that mapped a join to a fold was shown to fail three arms before this landed

claims.statement: The inferred-lineage fallback is OUT of the theorem.
claims.reason: where no transform tree has labelled a fact, the walk falls back to lineage inferred from evidence linkage, and that inference is sound only where a derivation was routed through a series output - a derivation that was not is invisible to it, and an invisible upstream carries no taint at all. The theorem covers the COMPUTED side. The shipped code raises a finding naming every fact it fell back on, precisely so a verdict resting on inference cannot pass for one resting on computation, and this exclusion exists so the ladder does not quietly promote it.

claims.statement: A hostile operator is OUT.
claims.reason: root access, memory dumps, a modified binary and a compromised host are outside every sentence in the proved rung, and no amount of information-flow proof reaches them. Closing that gap is a hardware-attestation question, not a theorem. Stated rather than omitted because an unstated exclusion reads, to whoever finds it later, as a claim that failed.

claims.statement: That every pipeline declares its sources honestly is OUT.
claims.reason: a source nobody declared labels as clean. That is a POSITIVE statement the composition makes - which contributor a source belongs to is knowledge the composition has and the frame does not - and nothing here can detect a declaration that was simply wrong.

claims.statement: That the transform algebra stays closed is OUT.
claims.reason: the shipped contribution function is an exhaustive match, so a sixth transform case fails to compile until someone says what it reads. That is production's guard, not this theorem's, and the model would have to gain the case too.

claims.statement: Over ANY sequence of pushes and pops, a well-formed ring produces exactly the outputs a reference FIFO queue produces from its unread contents, and ends well-formed holding exactly what the queue holds. Every pushed item is popped exactly once, in push order, however many times the ring grows on the way - fifo, no lost slot and no double pop in one statement.
Two items pushed in order are popped in that order, from the ring the constructor builds.
After any operation sequence from a fresh ring, the outputs are the reference queue's: no push is dropped and no slot is returned twice.
A pop on a well-formed ring never returns one of the placeholder slots the constructor and the grow step manufacture - `Unchecked.defaultof` is never observed as a value.

A push that triggers `doubleSize` leaves the unread contents in order with the pushed item last, in a ring of 2n + 1 slots whose read head is 0. The grow step is `2n + 1`, not `2n`: the inclusive `0 .. items.Length` range yields one placeholder more than the comment says, and the model reproduces it.

The precondition every ring theorem carries - at least two slots - is met by construction: `create` floors its capacity at `minimum_capacity` = 2, the ONE number `RingBuffer.MinimumCapacity` and `Program.withRingBufferCapacity` both read since 788.D. And it is necessary: at one slot the second push overwrites the first item before the grow step runs and the first pop returns the second item - `capacity_one_loses_an_item` is that execution, computed on the model with the floor bypassed.
The modelling step is faithful: the case-split index step the model uses IS `(i + 1) % n` on every index the code holds.
`toStart` holds exactly the deduplicated requested subs whose key is not active - as pairs, so the start function that survives dedup is the one the caller will run.
`toStop` holds exactly the active subs whose key is no longer requested.
`toKeep` holds exactly the active subs whose key is still requested, and with `toStop` partitions the active list.
No key is both started and stopped, and no key is both kept and stopped.
A key is reported as a duplicate iff it occurs more than once in the requested subs; the survivor is the LAST occurrence, because `List.foldBack` folds the last entry first.

When `keys = newKeys` the shortcut returns `dupes, [], active, []` - and the general path, run on the same input, returns the same four lists. The shortcut is an optimisation, not a different answer; this is where a started-twice / never-stopped leak would have lived.
After `change`, every active key is a requested key and - when every start succeeds - every requested key is active.

The extracted models agree with the production `RingBuffer` and `Sub.Internal.diff` / `Fx.change` over generated operation sequences (pushes, pops, grows past several doublings, full drains) and generated subscription sets (duplicates, the shortcut's exact-key-set case), on .NET - keys AND the identity of every handle and start function carried through.
